meta.title: Profile | Adittya Pratama
meta.description: Full-stack developer and system analyst at UPT TIK, Universitas Perjuangan Tasikmalaya, and the six-step process behind every change.

profile.title: I analyze the problem, then build the system.
profile.text: I design and run the systems students, faculty, and staff depend on every day, and I'm writing a master's thesis on applied retrieval.

workflow.title: How I work.
workflow.text: Six steps. The riskier the change, the more of them it gets.

steps.title: Rate the risk.
steps.text: A one-file tweak moves fast. Schema, money, access, or production changes get the full route.

steps.title: Read before touching.
steps.text: Entry points, data flow, business rules, and the database are mapped before old code changes.

steps.title: Plan, then one ticket at a time.
steps.text: Requirements become a written plan. Each ticket gets its own branch and is built test-first.

steps.title: Diagnose before fixing.
steps.text: A bug is reproduced and its cause evidenced before a single line changes.

steps.title: Review with fresh eyes.
steps.text: Medium and heavy changes get an independent second review before they merge.

steps.title: Ship with a way back.
steps.text: The release plan comes first. The write-up comes from what actually shipped.

items.title: Transactions first.
items.text: Schemas and transaction boundaries designed to prevent concurrency conflicts at enrollment peaks.

items.title: One source for the books.
items.text: Ledger postings, trial balances, and financial statements all come from the same double-entry engine.

items.title: Events, not guesses.
items.text: RabbitMQ and Redis carry game telemetry and session state in an event-driven design.

items.title: Operated, not just shipped.
items.text: Hardened Linux servers, Cloudflare edge rules, and automated database backups.

story.lead: Most institutional software fails slowly, in the places nobody checks.
paragraphs: A wrong balance, a duplicated enrollment, or a lost event rarely crashes anything. It sits in the records until someone needs them.
I work on the part that keeps those records true: schemas, transaction boundaries, and the checks around them. I analyze how the work really happens first, then build the system to match.
I like systems that stay in use, so I design for the day after launch.
